👤 User

Analyze the patent landscape in BindingDB.

🧠 Assistant

Data: BindingDB release 202610. A record counts as a patent when its source ID starts with US or WO (journals "US Patent" and "WIPO").

Scale

  • 8,998 patents: 7,265 granted US patents (B1/B2), 1,631 US applications (A1), 24 US reissues and 78 WO/PCT applications. Almost all are US documents published from 2013 on, when BindingDB started curating patents.
  • 1.36 M measurements (42% of BindingDB) and 688 k distinct compounds (47%), covering 3,213 of the 12,000 targets.
  • Patent chemical space barely overlaps the literature. Only 26 k patent compounds (3.8%) also appear in a journal article or other non-patent source. In practice, patents are a separate, mostly unpublished chemistry collection.
  • Since 2014, patents add more new compounds per year than journal articles do: 70–90 k per year against about 30 k (Figure 1). The drop in articles after 2023 is curation lag, not a real decline.
  • A typical patent reports 42 compounds (median; 90th percentile 247; maximum 2,689 in US12581252B2, PI3Kα). 61% of patents report data on only one target.

What is being patented

For each patent I took its lead target (the one with the most compounds measured), so that safety-panel targets don't inflate the counts. hERG and the CYP450s appear in more than 100 patents each, but almost always as off-targets.

Most-patented lead targets overall: BTK (182), BACE1 (103), JAK1 (85), IRAK4 (80), TYK2 (74), LSD1 (73), Nav1.7, RORγt and OX2R (72 each), FGFR1 and HDAC1 (70 each). If every target measured counts, the JAK family leads (JAK2 196, JAK1 183, JAK3 161), along with BTK (216).

Class mix (Figure 2):

  • Kinases are the largest single class and still growing, from about 23% to 28% of patents.
  • GPCRs fell from 18% to 7%, and proteases from 10% to 4.5%.
  • Epigenetic targets rose from about 2% to 8%.
  • Small but rising classes: E3 ligase / degrader patents (cereblon), phosphatases (almost all SHP2) and immuno-oncology targets. The immuno-oncology group (PD-L1, IDO1, STING, CD73) peaked around 2021 and is now declining.

Rising and falling targets (Figure 3)

Comparing 2013–17 with 2022–26:

  • Newly crowded: HPK1/MAP4K1 (0 → 44 patents), SARS-CoV-2 Mpro/pp1a (0 → 44) and pp1ab (0 → 34), cereblon (0 → 32), RIPK1 (1 → 33), small-molecule PD-1/PD-L1 (0 → 31), SHP2 (3 → 34), 5-HT2A (14 → 45, largely psychedelic-derived agonists for CNS indications), IRAK4, TYK2, DGKα and CDK2.
  • Largely abandoned: BACE1 (76 → 2) and PDE10A (51 → 2) after their clinical failures, plus Nav1.7 (40 → 6), OX2R, SYK, HCV, S1P1, c-MET, PIM1, κ-opioid and 11β-HSD1. BTK is still the largest lead target but has lost share (60 → 41).
  • Title keyword trends (2013–17 → 2022–26): degrader/PROTAC 11 → 111, KRAS 2 → 65, deuterated compounds 6 → 70, macrocycles 23 → 62, COVID 0 → 79. Pain (198 → 97) and psychiatric (200 → 99) patents roughly halved, while oncology patents grew from 620 to 1,095.

Saturation by target. For several targets, patents now hold most of the known chemistry: about 93% of all HPK1 compounds come from patents, about 91% for IRAK4, and 84–86% for OX2R, BTK and JAK1. Classic academic targets are the opposite: AChE, carbonic anhydrases and 5-HT1A are each under 7% patent-derived.

Potency and molecular properties (Figure 4)

  • Patent data are about 1 log unit more potent than literature data: median pIC50 7.0 vs 6.0, and median pKi 7.5 vs 6.7. 24% of patent IC50 values are 10 nM or better, compared with 13% in the literature. This reflects the bias of optimized patent series and claim-supporting examples.
  • Patent molecules are getting larger. The share above 500 Da rose from 24% (2014) to 43% (2025), and the median MW from 438 to 481. Patent compounds are also larger than literature compounds from the same period (median MW 466 vs 423). Degraders, macrocycles and KRAS/PPI chemistry drive the increase.

Caveats

  • BindingDB holds no assignee data, only inventor names, so this analysis cannot rank companies.
  • Coverage is essentially US-only and selective: these are patents BindingDB chose to curate, not the full patent record.
  • Patent "year" is the publication or grant year, so trends lag filing by 2–4 years. 2026 is a partial year.
  • Target classes come from keyword rules on target names, which are approximate (about a third of patents fall in "Other enzymes & proteins"). A few lead-target assignments are curation artifacts; for example, a TG2 patent is listed under MAP4K1.

Figure 1: Patents vs. journal literature in BindingDB, 2005–2026. Source documents (left) and distinct compounds (right) per year. Patent curation starts in 2013 and has supplied more compounds per year than journal articles since 2014. The shaded area marks curation lag for articles; 2026 is a partial year.

Figure 2: Target-class mix of patents over time. Share of patents per year by the class of each patent's lead target (the target with the most compounds measured in that patent). Classes were assigned by keyword rules on target names; each panel has its own y-scale.

Figure 3: Lead targets gaining and losing patent share. Change in the share of patents (percentage points) between 2013–2017 (2,755 patents) and 2022–2026 (3,403 patents), by lead target. The labels give the raw patent counts in each window.

Figure 4: Potency and molecular weight of patent compounds. Left: pAffinity distributions (Ki, Kd, IC50, EC50) for patent and non-patent measurements; the spikes at whole numbers come from values reported as round thresholds. Right: share of patent compounds with MW above 500 Da, by patent year.
